lesson.title: Token Passing: A Ticket That Guarantees Your Turn
lesson.summary: Token passing is a controlled access MAC scheme in which a single special frame, the token, circulates among stations and only the station currently holding it may transmit, eliminating collisions entirely at the cost of the delay and complexity of maintaining the token itself.
lesson.body:
Every MAC protocol examined so far, ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD, and CSMA/CA, belongs to the random access family: any station may attempt to transmit whenever it wants, and collisions are handled, or avoided, as a consequence rather than prevented structurally. Token passing takes a fundamentally different approach, controlled access, where the right to transmit is an explicit, exclusive permission that moves from station to station, so that at any given moment there is exactly one station in the entire network allowed to send. Because only one station can ever hold that permission, two stations transmitting data frames at the same time simply cannot happen. Token passing eliminates collisions by construction rather than by detecting or avoiding them statistically.

The permission itself is a small, distinctive control frame called the token, which carries no data, only a marker meaning it is now your turn. Stations are organized, logically if not always physically, into a sequence, most classically a ring, and the token passes from one station to the next around that sequence. A station that receives the token and has data to send seizes it, transmits its frame or frames, up to a limit called the token holding time so one busy station cannot monopolize the network, and then releases the token to the next station in sequence. A station that receives the token with nothing to send simply passes it along immediately, so idle stations do not slow the ring down.

This design gives token passing a property random access protocols cannot promise: a bounded, predictable worst case wait. Because the token visits every station in a fixed sequence, a station can calculate the maximum time it will wait before its turn comes around again, roughly the sum of every other station's token holding time plus the propagation delay around the ring. Under heavy, sustained load, this predictability lets token passing deliver higher effective throughput than CSMA based schemes, since no channel time is wasted on collisions, only the overhead of token circulation itself. CSMA and its variants, by contrast, degrade under heavy load precisely because more contending stations means more collisions and more time lost to backoff.

The tradeoff is operational fragility and latency for lightly loaded networks. If a station holding the token crashes or is disconnected before releasing it, the token can simply vanish, and the entire network loses its only means of granting transmission rights. Real systems need a recovery mechanism, typically a monitor station that detects a missing token after a timeout and regenerates one, adding complexity that CSMA based networks never need since they have no shared, mutable state like a token to lose. There is also a floor on delay even when the network is nearly idle: a station with a single frame to send may still have to wait for the token to complete its full circuit, however briefly each other station holds it, before its own turn comes.

Token Ring and Token Bus were the two major commercial implementations of this idea, competing directly against Ethernet's CSMA/CD through the 1980s and into the 1990s on the argument that guaranteed, collision free access mattered more than raw simplicity, particularly for industrial and time sensitive applications. Ethernet ultimately won the broader market on cost and simplicity, but token passing's core guarantee, exactly one transmitter at a time by construction rather than by policing after the fact, remains a clean illustration of the controlled access alternative to CSMA based schemes.
